overview:
Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world, after Vatican City: about two square kilometers of steep hillside and harbor squeezed between France and the Mediterranean Sea. A steady walker can cross the whole country in under an hour. Because there is so little land, Monaco builds upward and outward, stacking apartment towers up the cliffs and laying whole neighborhoods on ground reclaimed from the sea.

About 39,000 people live in the principality, and French is the official language, though Italian, English, and the old Monégasque dialect are all heard on the streets. Monaco is a principality governed by a prince of the Grimaldi family together with an elected council, one of the last places in Europe where a royal family still runs the country day to day. Its capital is Monaco itself.

The country is known worldwide for the Monte Carlo casino, a harbor packed with yachts, and the Monaco Grand Prix, a Formula One race driven through ordinary city streets, past hotels and around a famous hairpin turn.
landAndNature: Monaco sits on a narrow shelf of the French Riviera, where the Maritime Alps drop almost straight into the sea. The Rock of Monaco, a limestone headland, juts into the water and carries the prince's palace and the old town on its flat top. Winters are mild and summers hot and dry, a Mediterranean climate with sunshine most days of the year. Almost no wild land remains, but the Exotic Garden clings to a cliff face with thousands of cacti and succulents above a cave of stalactites, and the country protects patches of sea where seahorses, groupers, and meadows of posidonia seagrass grow.
peopleAndCulture: Only about a quarter of residents hold Monégasque citizenship; the rest come from France, Italy, and more than a hundred other countries, so several languages mix in any cafe. The food is Riviera food: barbagiuan, a fried pastry stuffed with chard and cheese, socca pancakes made from chickpea flour, and seafood straight off the boats. The Oceanographic Museum, once directed by the explorer Jacques Cousteau, hangs above the waves with sharks and coral in its tanks. Monaco's biggest days are the Grand Prix in May, a winter circus festival that draws acrobats from everywhere, and the national holiday on November 19. The soccer club AS Monaco plays in the French league.
history: People sheltered in caves along this coast in prehistoric times, and Greek settlers founded a town here around 2,500 years ago; the Romans later called the harbor Portus Herculis Monoeci. In 1297 François Grimaldi seized the fortress on the Rock, by tradition disguised as a monk, and the Grimaldi family has held it almost ever since, making them one of Europe's longest-ruling dynasties. Monaco spent centuries under Spanish and then French protection, and in 1861 it won full independence while giving up most of its territory. The casino that opened soon after rescued the treasury. In 1956 Prince Rainier III married the American film star Grace Kelly, and Monaco joined the United Nations in 1993.
funFacts: Monaco is smaller than New York's Central Park, yet it is a fully independent country with its own small army of about 120 soldiers.
The Grand Prix runs on public roads: barriers go up for the race, and days later the same streets carry ordinary traffic again.
Monaco is the most densely populated country on Earth, with roughly 19,000 people living in each square kilometer.
About a fifth of Monaco's land has been reclaimed from the sea, and new districts are still being built on the water.
Monégasque citizens are barred from gambling in the Monte Carlo casino, a rule that dates back to the casino's earliest years.
